newsitem.title: USA: Environmentalists want restructuring plan review.
newsitem.headline: Environmentalists want restructuring plan review.

text.p: A coalition of environmental organizations have filed with the New York State Public Service Commission seeking a complete review of the environmental impact of plans to restructure five of the state's electric utilities.

The coalition -- which includes Environmental Advocates, Natural Resources Defense Council, New York Public Interest Research Group and Pace Energy Project -- said Friday the commission must prepare a supplemental environmental impact statement before it can approve utility restructuring plans.

The group's statement charge that "with rare exceptions," the environmental review documents prepared by the utilities "have been treated by the utilities more as an annoyance to be dismissed summarily, than as a means of providing essential information."

Noting the reduced levels of spending for environmental measures called for by the company plans, as compared to the generic plan approved by the commission last year, NYPIRG senior attorney Larry Shapiro said state law requires preparation of a supplemental impact statement when plans change.
"Restructuring of the electric industry simply cannot move forward until after the PSC fully reviews the environmental impacts of those plans," Shapiro said.
The coalition's filing with the commission Wednesday preserves the group's right to seek court action if they do not like the regulatory response to their concerns, Shapiro explained.
"Customers can't make informed choices about electricity suppliers unless they known how the power is generated," added Peter Iwanowicz, project director for Environmental Advocates.
"Only Orange & Rockland (Utilities Inc ) plans to require disclosure of how much pollution is caused by these power plants," he said.

Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc, Central Hudson Gas and Electric Corp, New York State Electric and Gas Corp and Rochester Gas and Electric Corp "have submitted plans that would keep customers in the dark," he added.
